definition: Rationalize means to invent reasonable-sounding excuses for a choice or behavior.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rationalize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rationalize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: She rationalized skipping the reunion — too far, too formal — though the truth was a quarrel she didn't want to reopen.
To explain is milder than to rationalize — an explanation lays out what happened honestly, while rationalizing starts bending the reasons to flatter the chooser.
Whitewash goes further than rationalize: a rationalizer half-believes the excuses, while a whitewasher knowingly paints over the wrongdoing for others.

An excuse admits a fault and offers a reason meant to lessen the blame for it. To rationalize is to deny there was a fault at all: invented reasons dress the choice up as sensible. Excusing asks for pardon; rationalizing insists none is needed.

To justify is to argue honestly that the act was actually right, with reasons that are real and were true before the choice was made. Rationalize is its dishonest twin: the reasons arrive afterward and exist to flatter the chooser. Good reasons justify; manufactured ones rationalize.
to state the real reason plainly, blame and all
to accept an unflattering truth about yourself

Rationalize means to invent reasonable-sounding excuses for a choice or behavior.

After cutting the rookie, the manager rationalized the decision all winter: the kid was “a bad fit,” the roster “too crowded,” the timing “out of my hands” — every reason arriving conveniently after the choice, and none of them the misjudged tryout he never mentioned.
Rationalize is the accusing word here because the reasons were invented afterward to make a finished decision feel sound.
Explain would be neutral; justify would mean the reasons were honestly good.
Rationalize says the logic is decoration — reasonable-sounding, and reverse-engineered.

Aesop's fox wanted the grapes badly, leapt for them all afternoon, and could not reach them.
What he did next made the fable immortal.
He trotted off announcing that the grapes were obviously sour and he had never really wanted them.
Psychologists give the move a clinical name: the fox rationalized.
The wanting was real and the failure was real, but a reason was manufactured, after the fact, that made the outcome flattering.
A genuine reason exists before the choice; the fox's reason appeared only once the grapes were out of reach.
Two thousand years later the fable survives because the move does.
Nobody hears 'sour grapes' and needs the mechanics of the story retold.
